abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: While CRISPR has revolutionized biotechnology, predicting CRISPR-Cas nuclease activity remains a challenge. Herein, through the trans-cleavage feature of CRISPR-Cas12a, we investigate the correlation between CRISPR enzyme kinetics and the free energy change of crRNA and DNA targets from their initial thermodynamic states to a presumed transition state before hybridization. By subjecting computationally designed CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs), we unravel a linear correlation between the trans-cleavage kinetics of Cas12a and the energy barrier for crRNA spacer and single-stranded DNA target unwinding. This correlation shifts to a parabolic relationship with the energy consumption required for double-stranded DNA target separation. We further validate these correlations using ∼100 randomly selected crRNA/DNA pairs from viral genomes. Through machine learning methods, we reveal the synergistic effect of free energy change of crRNA and DNA on categorizing Cas12a activity on a two-dimensional map. Furthermore, by examining other potential factors, we find that the free energy change is the predominant factor governing Cas12a kinetics. This study will not only empower sequence design for numerous applications of CRISPR-Cas12a systems, but can also extend to activity prediction for a variety of enzymatic reactions driven by nucleic acid dynamics.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR) system, originally discovered as an acquired immunity mechanism for prokaryotes defending the infection of viruses (1,2), has reshaped the development of biotechnology owing to its exceptional feature of programmable nuclease activity. This has led to numerous applications in the fields of genome engineering (3–6), disease treatment and diagnosis (7–12), and multidisciplinary studies (13–17). The single-effector CRISPR system typically comprises a Cas endonuclease, a guide RNA (gRNA) containing a direct repeat region and a spacer region, and a nucleic acid target (either DNA or RNA). Mechanistic studies have revealed that the CRISPR system structurally recognizes the direct repeat region for pre-processing of gRNA (18–24), forming a Cas-gRNA ribonucleoprotein (RNP) and stabilizing the conformation of several domains in the Cas endonucleases (25). Subsequently, the spacer region directs the RNP to a complementary DNA or RNA target (2,20,22,24). The binding between gRNA and the target induces conformational changes (20,25,26) of the Cas endonuclease and activation of its nuclease domain, resulting in site-specific cleavage of targeted nucleic acids, termed cis-cleavage (2,26,27). For type V and VI CRISPR-Cas systems, beyond cis-cleavage, the exposed nuclease domain also catalyzes indiscriminate degradation of surrounding single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) for Cas12a and single-stranded RNA for Cas13a, termed trans-cleavage (10,28).

Because CRISPR-mediated cleavage of nucleic acids is programmable by altering the spacer sequence of gRNA, the reaction efficiency is sequence-dependent and may vary across orders of magnitude when targeting different sequences (29). Therefore, it is essential to explore the interconnections between target sequence and reaction kinetics for a deeper understanding of the CRISPR reaction mechanism and to provide more insightful guidance on target selection for a higher reaction efficiency. Previous work has largely focused on the cis-cleavage activity possessed by Cas9 and Cas12a. Such studies have identified key features that might influence the frequency of insertions and deletions (indels) in both in vitro and in vivo contexts. These features include, but are not limited to, the GC content (29–32), the nucleotide frequency at each position (31,33–35), and the nucleotide preference at the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM)-proximal seed region (29,30,32,34–37) and at the cleavage site (37). However, trans-cleavage may serve as a more ideal model for characterizing nuclease kinetics, as it can be recorded in real time and uses a constant substrate sequence, thus excluding interferences introduced by substrate variations. By simply labeling uniform substrates with a fluorophore-quencher pair (FQ) (10), the reaction speed can be directly measured through real-time fluorescence monitoring, without the need to infer it from indirect measurements such as indel frequency (29,32–34,36–38) and protein expression levels (30,31,37). Moreover, the trans-cleavage feature enables molecular diagnostics of various diseases (10,11,39–41), an application scenario where target selection is more flexible compared to genome editing, rendering the prediction of trans-cleavage kinetics particularly significant.

Given that the initiation of Cas12a nuclease activity is induced by the hybridization of crRNA and the DNA target, which allosterically unlocks the RuvC nuclease domain (25,26), we infer that the kinetics of crRNA–DNA hybridization is a predominant factor influencing the kinetics of Cas12a nuclease activity. Since the principal rate-determining step of hybridization is the unwinding of the participating nucleic acids, the original secondary structure and the folding energy of these nucleic acids are believed to be strongly correlated with the reaction kinetics (42,43).

In this work, we aim to investigate how Cas12a nuclease kinetics, as reflected by trans-cleavage rates, is associated with the free energy change of nucleic acids involved. We began by algorithmically designing crRNAs for the Cas12a system with varying numbers of stable base pairs in the spacer region. A wide range of GC content (20−80%) were applied in target generation. We analyzed both ssDNA and double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) targets, experimentally testing a total of 123 crRNA species. Remarkably, the data suggested a linear correlation between the trans-cleavage rate and the free energy change of crRNA spacers and ssDNA targets, transitioning from their original states to unwound states where the targeting sites were fully exposed. For dsDNA targets, the change in free energy from the hybridized state to the separated state exhibited a quasi-parabolic relationship with the trans-cleavage rate, with an optimal range of free energy change observed. Leveraging machine learning-based clustering and classification, we clearly delineated zones of free energy change of crRNA/DNA pairs demonstrating varying levels of nuclease potency on a two-dimensional (2D) map, potentially assisting in target selection for CRISPR-based diagnostics and other applications. Moreover, we speculate that the energy consumption of crRNA and DNA unwinding for targeting site exposure is the major determinant of Cas12a nuclease activity, as the other analyzed features consistently showed vague correlations. Overall, our findings have the potential to provide a mechanistic understanding of CRISPR and shed light on many other enzymatic reactions from an energy perspective.

sec.title: Computational crRNA design
sec.p: The generation of crRNA sequences with hairpin and linear spacers was achieved by a customized algorithm empowered by the ViennaRNA Package, written in Python 3. Candidate 20-nt RNA sequences with a certain GC content were randomly generated and subjected to the following screening criteria: (1) If the minimum free energy (MFE) structure of the entire crRNA (including the direct repeat) coincided with the predefined secondary structure; (2) If every base pair in the spacer had a base pairing probability of no less than 95%. For species with eight base pairs in the spacer, achieving the expected probability of base pairing between the first and last bases in the spacer might be difficult; hence, we lowered the threshold to 75%; (3) If every unpaired base in the spacer had a base pairing probability lower than 5% to any other bases in the spacer or any unpaired bases in the direct repeat; (4) If every base pair in the direct repeat had a base pairing probability of no less than 99%. As reaching the expected base pairing probability of the first base pair counting from the 5′ end in the direct repeat might be difficult, we lowered the threshold to 85%. In particular, the design of crRNA with linear spacers adopted stricter criteria, where the base pairing probability of any two bases in the spacer was less than 1%, and the MFE frequency of the entire crRNA was no less than 80%. sec.title: Recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) primer design
sec.p: RPA primer design was enabled by Primer3 and NUPACK 4.0 and implemented in Python 3. A primer pair consisting of forward and reverse primers, each 32 nucleotides long, was randomly generated and subjected to the following screening criteria: (1) If the GC content was between 45 and 55%; (2) If the MFE structure at the reaction temperature (39°C) was linear, with an MFE frequency of no less than 25%; (3) If the melting temperature of any possible hairpin loop fr /ormed was below 20°C; (4) If the melting temperature of any possible homodimer formed was below 20°C; (5) If the melting temperature of any possible heterodimer formed between the forward and reverse primers was below 20°C; (6) If the sequence overlap between a primer and the assembled plasmid (including vector, candidate forward primer, eight targets, and candidate reverse primer) or its reverse complement was fewer than 10 nucleotides; (7) If the sequence overlap between a target and the assembled plasmid or its reverse complement was fewer than 10 nucleotides; (8) If the Hamming distance between a primer and any 32-nucleotide segment of the assembled plasmid was greater than 13 (meaning more than 13 bases of difference); (9) If the Hamming distance between a target and any 20-nucleotide segment of the assembled plasmid was greater than 1 (meaning more than 1 base of difference; single-base mismatches were not tolerated). The designed spacer sequences also adhered to diversity constraints, where every four bases contained at least two nucleotide types and every six bases contained at least one base from ‘A/T’ and one base from ‘G/C’. The full list of designed RPA primer sequences for every plasmid tested can be found in the ‘Table of sequences’ section of the Supplementary Information.

sec.title: Computation of free energy changes
sec.p: The computation of free energy changes was primarily accomplished using NUPACK 4.0 for all DNA species and the ViennaRNA Package for all crRNA species, utilizing scripts written in Python 3. Assuming the free energy of oligonucleotides in the defined ‘linear’ state without any self-folding is 0, the free energy change of short ssDNA targets from their original states to the ‘linear’ state then equals the ensemble free energy.

For long ssDNA targets, the free energy change for a specified structure was defined as the difference between the free energy of the entire strand when the targeting region was in its original state and when it was in the ‘linear’ state. The overall free energy change was ideally the weighted sum of free energy change for all suboptimal structures.

sec.title: Trans-cleavage assay of CRISPR-Cas12a
sec.p: The CRISPR reaction mixture used in the trans-cleavage assay consisted of 300 nM of EnGen® Lba Cas12a (Cpf1) (New England Biolabs, Cat# M0653T) or 300 nM of Alt-R™ A.s. Cas12a (Cpf1) V3 (Integrated DNA Technologies, Cat# 1 081 068), 1 × NEBuffer™ r3.1 (New England Biolabs, Cat# B6003S), 12 nM of crRNA, 5 μM of ssDNA-FQ (5′-FAM-TTATT-IABkFQ-3′) and DNA targets. For short and long ssDNA testing, serially diluted targets at concentrations of 60 nM, 6 nM and 600 pM were used. For unamplified dsDNA testing, plasmid and λDNA (Thermo Scientific™, Cat# SD0021) at a concentration of 6 nM were used. For RPA-amplified dsDNA testing, the plasmid template at 5 fM or 500 aM was first amplified using the TwistAmp® Basic kit (TwistDx™ Limited, Cat# TABAS03KIT) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Specifically, one RPA reaction in a total volume of 50 μL contained 29.5 μL of primer-free rehydration buffer, 2.4 μL of 10 μM forward primer, 2.4 μL of 10 μM reverse primer, 2.5 μL of 280 mM magnesium acetate, 2.5 μL of template and 13.2 μL of nuclease-free water. The reaction was incubated at 39°C for 20 min. After that, 1.5 μL of amplicon was added to the CRISPR reaction mixture under a PCR workstation (AirClean Systems) to avoid cross-contamination. The CRISPR reaction in a total volume of 25 μL was incubated at 37°C in the CFX96 Touch Real-Time PCR Detection System (Bio-Rad Laboratories) for 1 h of fluorescence monitoring with a recording interval of 15 s. All the synthetic oligonucleotides and genes, including crRNAs, short ssDNA targets, long ssDNA targets, plasmids, and RPA primers, used in this study were obtained from Integrated DNA Technologies. The sequences are listed in the ‘Table of sequences’ section of the Supplementary Information. The trans-cleavage assay on every crRNA/DNA pair was performed in triplicate, and the data used in fitting, 2D color map construction, and machine learning were the average values from all three experiments.

sec.title: Machine learning for energy zone division
sec.p: All machine learning approaches for energy zone division were implemented using the built-in algorithms in scikit-learn (44). For K-means clustering, all input energy data were applied in the fitting, and we calculated the mean value of the trans-cleavage data in each cluster as the basis for ranking the divided energy zones. The optimal number of clusters was determined primarily according to the distribution of the trans-cleavage data in each cluster, whether they could be clearly segregated among clusters, and whether the division of energy zones coincided with our presumptions from the previous analysis, with the elbow method (45), silhouette score (46), and Calinski–Harabasz index (47) serving as auxiliary assessments of clustering quality. For the classification methods employed, the labeling of trans-cleavage data was derived from the quartile ranking of the differences in logarithm values of the trans-cleavage rates compared to the highest within the same target type. The input data were randomly split into 80% for the training set and 20% for the testing set, and the models selected to generate energy zone divisions were those that yielded the highest accuracy scores after 10 000 independent fittings with Gaussian-naive Bayes, SVM, LDA, and logistic regression, and 1000 independent fittings with the neural network. The kernel type used in SVM was linear, as we hypothesized that ideally the data points can be separated into distinct classes with linear boundaries on the map. The solver used to optimize the objective function was singular value decomposition for LDA and the limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno algorithm for logistic regression. For the neural network, the solver was stochastic gradient descent, and the activation function for the hidden layer with 20 neurons was rectified linear unit.

sec.title: Overview and computational crRNA design
sec.p: To more intuitively represent the stepwise increase of free energy change and its impact on Cas12a nuclease kinetics, we computationally designed crRNA spacers that meet specific structural criteria, including those steadily self-hybridized with varying numbers of base pairs and those that were stably unfolded. To avoid possible negative effects induced by irregular structures of the direct repeat or unwanted base-pairing between the direct repeat and spacer (48), every base in the direct repeat region of the designed crRNA, whether paired or unpaired, followed the canonical structure (24) and had a probability higher than 85% to maintain the pairing condition under the predicted minimum free energy (MFE) structure (Supplementary Figure S1). The 20-nt spacer was designed as a hairpin with four bases making up the loop. The degree of spacer self-hybridization was represented by the number of base pairs in the stem. In this study, we started with eight base pairs in the stem, where no bases were unpaired except those in the loop, and designed crRNAs with sequentially reducing base pairs until reaching three base pairs, as stems comprising fewer base pairs were unstable and computationally difficult to design. Additionally, we designed crRNAs with linear spacers to serve as the standard for comparison with those containing hairpin spacers (Figure 1A). Given the implication from previous research that GC content might play a role in CRISPR guide activity (43), we designed crRNA spacers with varying degrees of self-hybridization with four levels of GC content ranging from 20 to 80% (i.e. 20 or 25%, 40, 60 and 80%). To ensure the stability of the spacer structure, most bases in the spacer region were designed to have a probability higher than 95% of maintaining the pairing condition under the MFE structure (Supplementary Figure S1). Since all bases were confirmed to have a stable pairing condition, the MFE frequency of most designed crRNAs could easily reach above 80% (Supplementary Figure S1), indicating that the majority of crRNAs would be in the MFE state, possessing the intended structure. These criteria were initially established for designing crRNAs for AsCas12a, but we found that in most cases, crRNAs with an alternative direct repeat sequence for LbCas12a also satisfied these criteria. A full list of crRNA sequences can be found in the Supporting Information.

sec.p: To characterize the effect of oligo self-folding more accurately, we transformed the secondary structure of the oligo to the free energy of its thermodynamic ensemble, where lower free energy corresponds to a more stable state that generally involves more base pairings. We defined the free energy change of the crRNA when its spacer conformationally changes from its original state () to the ‘linear’ state () as . The ‘linear’ state is a transition state where the secondary structure of the spacer is unwound to be ready for hybridization to a complementary DNA strand. Correspondingly, the free energy change of the DNA when its targeting region switches from its original state () to the ‘linear’ state () was defined as . These free energy gaps can also be considered the Gibbs energy of activation between the ground state and the transition state of reacting nucleic acids (49).

Using the crRNAs designed above, we investigated the conditions when the target is ssDNA or dsDNA (PAM included) (Figure 1B). The studies on ssDNA were further divided into two categories: i) cases with short ssDNA, where the complete 20-nt sequence served as the target, and ii) cases where the 20-nt target was included in a long ssDNA strand. The intention of using long ssDNA was to confirm that the Cas12a nuclease activity was solely related to the free energy change of the targeting region of DNA. Additionally, the use of long ssDNA enriched the diversity of structures associated with a specific target sequence, providing examples where the target structure was not strongly correlated with the spacer structure. We also categorized the studies on dsDNA into cases with unamplified targets cloned in a plasmid and cases with recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA)-amplified targets, which better simulated practical applications in nucleic acid detection. We hypothesized that secondary structures severely hamper the hybridization of two strands (42), potentially decelerating trans-cleavage activity in the Cas12a system. Consequently, faster trans-cleavage kinetics should be more likely observed with linear spacers and targets (Figure 1C).

sec.title: Effect of free energy change on the trans-cleavage rate with ssDNA targets
sec.p: We began the investigation with the simplest target type: short ssDNA, which included only the targeting region completely complementary to the crRNA (Figure 2A). At a target concentration of 60 nM, we observed that crRNAs with more hybridized bases in the stem of the spacer tended to produce weaker fluorescence responses, indicating milder trans-cleavage activity (Figure 2B). Surprisingly, a significant number of crRNAs with multiple base pairs in the spacer, such as the ‘8_pair’ groups, where GC contents of 20, 60 and 80% generated almost imperceptible fluorescence response. However, with the number of base pairs in the spacer reduced to 4 or fewer, the groups with all GC contents were able to generate comparable fluorescence responses to those with linear spacers. These results were consistent with our anticipation that the secondary structures of crRNAs would be closely related to Cas12a nuclease activity.

sec.p: We then individually analyzed the impact of free energy change of both the target and crRNA spacer on the trans-cleavage rate. Strikingly, we found a strong linear correlation between and the base-10 logarithm of the trans-cleavage rate for both the target and spacer (Figure 2C, D), with the Pearson correlation coefficient describing the linearity with reaching 0.94. To further verify this finding, we obtained trans-cleavage rates with 10 × and 100 × diluted targets (at 6 nM and 600 pM, respectively) (Supplementary Figure S2A, B) and performed the same linear fitting and correlation analysis. We found that the linear correlation between the logarithm of the trans-cleavage rate and either or still existed but became weaker (Supplementary Figure S2C–F) when lowering the target concentration, suggesting that insufficient target might influence the hybridization kinetics and cause interference in predicting the trans-cleavage rate using a single factor.

In binarily categorizing the targets into ‘good performing’ ones and ‘bad performing’ ones based on their trans-cleavage rates, we wondered whether adjusting the energy threshold would shift the probability of observing a ‘good’ target. We defined a ‘good’ target as one having a trans-cleavage rate no lower than 50% of the highest trans-cleavage rate observed among all tested targets. A 50% reduction in the trans-cleavage rate implies the reaction time needs to be doubled to reach the same fluorescence intensity, which may greatly delay result generation for applications utilizing the trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a. We calculated the proportion of ‘good’ targets under a defined upper bound. As shown in Figure 2E, F, the ratio of a ‘good’ target was 0 when the upper bound of was −3 kcal/mol or lower, or when the upper bound of was −7 kcal/mol or lower. This result indicates that targets in these free energy change ranges were unlikely to have a trans-cleavage rate approaching the most ideal one and should be avoided in selection. As the threshold increased, the probability of observing a ‘good’ target rose concurrently. For lower target concentrations, the ratio of ‘good’ targets generally exhibited a similar rising trend with the upper bound of gradually elevating, despite more appearances of plateaus and even noticeable declines (Supplementary Figure S2G–J), which coincided with the conclusion made from the linear fittings that the correlation between and the trans-cleavage rate became weaker when using lower target concentrations. Finally, we plotted the base-10 logarithm of the trans-cleavage rate where and co-existed as variables (Figure 2G). As expected, the lowest trans-cleavage rates gathered at the lower-left corner of the figure where both and were lower, and relatively higher trans-cleavage rates were more frequently observed at the upper-right corner where both and were higher (Figure 2G, Supplementary Figure S2K, L).

To enable a more direct and reliable comparison between crRNAs with hairpin spacers and linear spacers, we designed a series of long ssDNA targets. Each target integrated eight short target sequences, with half matching the hairpin spacers and the other half matching the linear spacers. This design eliminated the interferences caused by possible concentration variation among tested targets. Additionally, it diversified nucleic acid secondary structures, especially for targets matching linear spacers. For long ssDNA targets, only the free energy change of the crRNA targeting region was considered as (Figure 2H). Consistent with the results with short ssDNA targets, trans-cleavage with linear spacers was stronger than with hairpin spacers in the same long target, and as the number of base pairs in the stem of the spacer increased, the difference in trans-cleavage rates became more apparent (Figure 2I). In particular, the trans-cleavage rates remained low for ‘8_pair’ and ‘7_pair’ hairpin spacers with all GC contents tested. Similar to the analysis in short ssDNA studies, we calculated the Pearson correlation coefficients using all 48 data points obtained to measure the relationship between and the average logarithm of trans-cleavage rates. The results suggested that and were still linearly correlated with the trans-cleavage rate (Figure 2J, K), although seemed to be less correlated compared to the short ssDNA cases. We reasoned that as the target became longer, the possibilities of suboptimal secondary structures might sharply rise, resulting in uniformly low frequencies for specified structures. Despite considering major suboptimal structures with free energies close to that of the MFE structure, the calculated values for long ssDNA were still not as accurate as the computed for ssDNA and , which deteriorated the fitting results. Longer sequences might also introduce off-target sites, which could mistakenly consume crRNAs and complicate the reaction kinetics. By calculating the ratio of ‘good’ targets under different thresholds (Figure 2L, M), we found that the upper bound of under which no ‘good’ targets were observed in long ssDNA, was almost identical to the results with short ssDNA targets. Finally, Figure 2N clearly demonstrates that low trans-cleavage rates concentrated at the bottom of figure, which correspond to low and , while higher trans-cleavage rates appeared more at the upper-right corner, corresponding to higher and . With diluted long ssDNA targets, the variations in trans-cleavage rates between the hairpin spacer and linear spacer diminished (Supplementary Figure S3A, B), as did the correlation between and trans-cleavage rates (Supplementary Figure S3C–F). This was consistent with the experimental observations with short ssDNA targets at low concentrations. In addition, the trend of the ratio of ‘good’ targets became more irregular, especially when the threshold was approaching 0 (Supplementary Figure S3G–J). We also noticed that the optimal thresholds of were not exactly 0 but rather −2 kcal/mol or −1 kcal/mol. As crRNA was excessive in this condition, we speculate that a perfectly linear spacer compromising trans-cleavage activity may be attributed to fast crRNA consumption due to non-specific hybridization between themselves or with random sequences from the target, as the energy expense for this unanticipated targeting was negligible. This effect potentially contributed to the reduced efficiency of binding between crRNA and the correct targeting site.

When using AsCas12a, another commonly available Cas12a ortholog, we observed considerable background fluorescence signals with all crRNAs tested (Supplementary Figure S4A, B), particularly with the ‘20_8_pair’ crRNA. This finding supports our recent discovery that Cas12a is RNA-activable (50) and strengthens our hypothesis that crRNAs might self-interact and disturb the regular nuclease activation mechanism. However, the background signals were not apparent when testing with LbCas12a (Supplementary Figure S4C, D). For a more accurate measurement with AsCas12a, we subtracted the background signal induced by crRNA itself (Supplementary Figure S5A–C) and obtained similar patterns of correlation between and the logarithm of the trans-cleavage rate (Supplementary Figure S5D–O), where ‘bad’ crRNA/DNA pairs aggregated at the lower-left corner of the map and ‘good’ pairs tended to group at the upper-right corner (Supplementary Figure S5P–R).

sec.title: Effect of free energy change on the trans-cleavage rate with dsDNA targets
sec.p: We next transitioned to dsDNA targets, a more common nucleic acid type in molecular detection and various other applications. Initially, we investigated cases with unamplified dsDNA targets cloned in a plasmid, with a PAM prefixed to every target sequence (Figure 3A). Due to limitations in product yield, we were only able to test the target-carrying plasmid at a single concentration that was high enough for the trans-cleavage signal to be measurable and analyzable. Consistent with the results obtained with ssDNA targets, crRNA spacers with a higher degree of self-hybridization were typically associated with lower trans-cleavage responses (Figure 3B). A few crRNA/DNA pairs produced almost undetectable fluorescence responses, particularly those with many base pairs in the spacer region and a high GC content. It is notable that the crRNA species producing negligible fluorescence responses in the dsDNA detection setting were not entirely the same as those in the short ssDNA detection setting, and there was a slight variation of good-performing crRNA species between these two detection settings. Considering that the free energy changes of dsDNA and ssDNA targets may not be strongly correlated even with the same targeting sequence, we believe the potency of trans-cleavage activity is less likely governed by the sequence itself and more closely associated with the energy characteristics.

sec.p: While a linear correlation between and the logarithm of the trans-cleavage rate still existed for the tested unamplified dsDNA targets (Supplementary Figure S6A, B), crRNA/dsDNA pairs with good performances appeared more frequently at an intermediate , specifically within the range from −26 to −22 kcal/mol (Supplementary Figure S6C). By further defining a threshold of at −4 kcal/mol, we were able to locate the energy region that included most crRNA/dsDNA pairs with high trans-cleavage potency (Supplementary Figure S6C). This optimal energy region was confirmed as it exhibited the highest mean value of reaction rates for all targets included (Supplementary Figure S6D). Interestingly, with an inference that of dsDNA couples with GC content, we found that the range of optimal matched a GC content of 35−55% (Supplementary Figure S6E), which was close to the empirically ideal range of GC content from cis-cleavage studies (30,31,36). Nevertheless, the sample size of crRNA/dsDNA pairs in the optimal energy region and its high neighborhood were not abundant enough to solidify this finding. To supplement, we selected 32 additional targets from the genomes of viruses causing major epidemics, including SARS-CoV-2, HIV-1, HPV 16, and HPV 18. These crRNA/target pairs were purposely selected with a high above -4 kcal/mol. To enable a clearer comparison, we further divided the energy regions where these targets were categorized into four levels based on and three levels based on , totaling 12 subregions. Each subregion with extreme (<−26 kcal/mol or >−22 kcal/mol) contained two targets and each subregion with intermediate (>−26 kcal/mol and <−22 kcal/mol) contained four targets (Supplementary Figure S6F). All targets were selected without additional constraints on sequence features. As expected, the selected targets uniformly exhibited strong trans-cleavage activity, with only a few showing below-average performance (Supplementary Figure S6G).

Taking into consideration both the designed and selected crRNA/dsDNA pairs, we found that the correlation between the logarithm of the trans-cleavage rate and remained linear (Figure 3C). Consistent with our observation that dsDNA targets with an intermediate empirically yielded better results, the trend of trans-cleavage activity with respect to became more parabolic, with the vertex appearing at a within the range anticipated to be optimal (Figure 3D). Moreover, while the ratio of ‘good’ targets kept increasing as the upper bound of elevated (Figure 3E), there was a slight but stable decline regarding the upper bound of starting at −22 kcal/mol (Figure 3F), suggesting that targets with a greater than −22 kcal/mol might less likely be ‘good’ targets compared to those with a in the optimal range (−27 to −22 kcal/mol), where the ratio of ‘good’ targets rapidly grew. Finally, the color map showing the logarithm of the trans-cleavage rates for dsDNA targets confirmed that stronger trans-cleavage activity commonly grouped in a region with high and moderate (Figure 3G).

Since the trans-cleavage property is often applied in point-of-care nucleic acid detection, which requires an isothermal pre-amplification step, we also studied the energy effect on RPA amplicons containing the dsDNA targets mentioned above (Figure 3H). Using amplicons may also improve the accuracy of analysis since amplicons exclusively comprise target sequences to be studied, mitigating the interferences introduced from the other sequences in the plasmid vector. The major challenge preventing the comparison of trans-cleavage activities among amplicons is the possible discrepancy in amplification efficiency, which can cause variations in the final concentrations of products. Considering the recommended amplicon length (100−200 bp) for RPA reactions (51), we adopted the same configuration for the study of long ssDNA targets. Each amplicon of designed targets included four targets matching hairpin crRNA spacers with the same degree of self-hybridization and four targets matching linear spacers. The targets matching linear spacers across different plasmids were identical, serving as a control to evaluate the amplification efficiency for every plasmid. By rational design of RPA primers (52,53) (see Methods) to ensure minimal hindrance in the amplification process and minimal coincidence with the complete assembled plasmid sequence, the amplification efficiency of the six plasmids we tested was homogeneous, even with different primers pairs applied. The deviations of the logarithm of the trans-cleavage rates for one target across different plasmids were all within ± 10% of the mean value (Supplementary Figure S7A).

Once again, the trans-cleavage data suggested that for every amplicon, targets matching a linear spacer—particularly those with a GC content of 40 or 60%—typically initiated stronger trans-cleavage activity than those matching a hairpin spacer (Figure 3I). Using the mean values of the logarithms of the trans-cleavage rates for targets matching linear spacers, we obtained a similar correlation between trans-cleavage activity and as that of unamplified targets (Supplementary Figure S7B, C). Additionally, we observed better performance occurring in the anticipated optimal energy region (Supplementary Figure S7D, E). Incorporating the results with the 32 selected targets after RPA (Supplementary Figure S7F), we concluded that the pattern of the relationship between or and the logarithm of the trans-cleavage rate for RPA-amplified dsDNA targets was the same as that for unamplified dsDNA targets (Figure 3J − M). Poorly performing crRNA/dsDNA pairs aggregated at the lower-left corner of the map, while top-performing ones appeared more frequently in the upper-middle region (Figure 3N). We also performed the same set of measurements and analysis on 10-fold diluted plasmid templates (500 aM), which generally resulted in a reduction of trans-cleavage rates by half. However, the conclusions were not significantly altered (Supplementary Figure S8).

sec.title: Machine learning-based division of energy zones by trans-cleavage activity
sec.p: The aforementioned findings suggest that the reactivity of crRNA/DNA pairs tends to be strongly correlated with the free energy change of interacting molecules. We hypothesized that by integrating machine learning techniques for categorizing the obtained data, a more accurately characterized relationship between free energy change and trans-cleavage performance could be revealed. As a demonstration, we initially used K-means clustering to segregate all spacer/target pairs tested in the unamplified dsDNA study and obtained the distribution of trans-cleavage reactivity in each divided energy zone. As the number of cluster increased, the lowest values of trans-cleavage rates became stably aggregated in the cluster corresponding to low values of and . The distinction in the distributions of trans-cleavage data among other clusters evolved to be clear (Supplementary Figure S9A–D). Subsequently, we divided the entire 2D field of and into six energy zones, which more evenly split crRNA/DNA pairs into high and low clusters. We observed that the trans-cleavage activity for targets in Clusters #1 − 3, which generally had higher , was significantly stronger than those in Clusters #4 − 6, which had lower . Consistent with the previous analysis, both the average and median trans-cleavage data among clusters indicated that dsDNA targets with an intermediate (around -26 to -22 kcal/mol) were the most ideal choices for the fastest trans-cleavage response. These were followed by targets with low and then targets with high (Supplementary Figure S9E). To validate this finding and supplement more data for the training of machine learning models, we further performed trans-cleavage assays on 62 targets in λDNA, a long phage DNA containing plenty of available Cas12a targeting sites prefixed with PAM. The quantity of selected targets in each cluster was kept approximately identical at 10 or 11, except more targets were included in Cluster #1, as more targets gathered in Cluster #1 in the previous experiment, and fewer targets were selected for Cluster #6 due to limited choices. We calculated the mean values of logarithms of trans-cleavage rates for all targets in each cluster and found that the originally defined Cluster #1 still yielded the highest trans-cleavage activity on average (Supplementary Figure S10A). More strikingly, we found that the ranking of the mean value of new trans-cleavage data mostly followed the order of cluster indexes obtained from the previous experiment, except for higher-than-expected trans-cleavage activity in Cluster #4, likely due to the inevitable selection of targets close to the border of Cluster #1, which were unrepresentative. As the cluster index became larger, the probability of observing a ‘good’ target, which had ≥ 50% reactivity of the highest, roughly exhibited a decreasing trend (Supplementary Figure S10B).

With an enlarged dataset combining the previous 61 targets and the new 62 targets from λDNA, we re-performed K-means clustering to possibly seek a more accurate division of energy zones based on trans-cleavage rates. The general applicability of this dataset was demonstrated through the observation of similar distributions of many factors that may influence CRISPR activity for a broader set of CRISPR target in the complete genome (Supplementary Figure S11). Meanwhile, for the ssDNA analysis, we integrated data from short and long targets to increase the sample size to 77. To reconcile the standard for comparison of trans-cleavage reactivity with different target types (i.e. synthetic plasmid and λDNA, short ssDNA targets and long ssDNA targets), we calculated the difference in logarithm values of trans-cleavage rates for every target compared to the highest one observed within one target type as the input for machine learning models. For ssDNA targets at relatively higher concentrations, the energy zone encompassing crRNA/DNA pairs with an average trans-cleavage reactivity closest to the peak was confined to the upper-right corner of the map as the cluster number grew (Supplementary Figure S12A–E) and became stabilized to a near-rectangular zone bordered by = −2.0 kcal/mol and = -2.0 kcal/mol (Figure 4A). For lower target concentrations, the optimal energy zone shifted downward to slightly lower areas, particularly when the molar ratio between crRNA and target was heavily unbalanced (1 : 0.05), potentially suggesting that high was not favored in this situation, as a considerable portion of crRNA with easily accessible spacer was consumed by random targeting (Supplementary Figure S12F–O). For K-means clustering on dsDNA targets, the energy zone corresponding to the strongest trans-cleavage activity gradually stabilized into an irregular quadrilateral (Supplementary Figure S13), with ranging from −25.9 to −21.3 kcal/mol at its widest, and no lower than −4.9 kcal/mol (Figure 4B).

sec.p: To enable the prediction of trans-cleavage performance based on free energy changes, we labeled the data based on quartile ranking of logarithms of trans-cleavage rates and assessed multiple supervised learning methods for their classification accuracy. The threshold trans-cleavage activity for each label can be found in Supplementary Figure S14. With the assumption that trans-cleavage activity varies uniformly with free energy change, we selected classification methods including naive Bayes, support vector machine (SVM), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), logistic regression, and neural network classification. These methods produced smooth edges for every energy zone with the lowest probability of generating discontinuous zones. The highest accuracy score for prediction of trans-cleavage activity with both ssDNA and dsDNA targets was achieved by naive Bayes (Figure 4C, D, Supplementary Figure S15). For ssDNA targets abundant in the reaction, the classification result (Figure 4C) clearly showed that was a more predominant factor in stratifying the trans-cleavage data when they were moderately high. The top three energy zones were almost horizontally segregated, and the naive Bayes model defined a narrower optimal region with a rigid restriction on not exceeding −0.4 kcal/mol. However, was more deterministic in identifying the least-active targets, as no targets were classified into higher levels if was less than −7.9 kcal/mol, regardless of the value of . When ssDNA targets were less abundant or deficient, the optimal region leaned toward lower (Supplementary Figure S15), in accordance with the K-means clustering results. For dsDNA targets, the naive Bayes classification suggested the optimal energy zone confined to with the widest range from −28.3 to −22.9 kcal/mol, moving leftward compared with the K-means clustering results, likely attributed to the involvement of more targets in the second-most reactive zone indicated by K-means clustering, while the lowest tolerable (-5.0 kcal/mol) remained almost unchanged (Figure 4D). Similar to ssDNA classification, below a certain level (-6.7 kcal/mol) defined a region where targets were considered to be the least reactive. These computed energy thresholds from the combined dataset can also adapt to individual datasets where the average trans-cleavage activity and the ratio of ‘good’ targets decreased with larger label numbers (Supplementary Figure S16). Other classification methods, albeit with lower accuracy scores, exhibited a similar division of energy zones regarding all concentrations of ssDNA and dsDNA targets (Supplementary Figure S17).

Leveraging the division of energy zones by naive Bayes, we studied the distribution of targets of a complete viral genome regarding their predicted trans-cleavage activity, aiming to provide a preliminary basis for target selection for CRISPR-based diagnostics. We analyzed all 20-nt sequences downstream of a canonical PAM (i.e. TTTV) in both the sense and antisense strand of 16 representative viral genomes causing human diseases (Figure 4E). We found that while the majority of targets were positioned in the best or the second-best energy zones, there were still a few predicted to have unsatisfactory reactivity, with kinetics around 47% or slower compared to the most ideal targets (Supplementary Figure S14B). This could significantly delay result interpretation for point-of-care testing. A count of classified targets in every energy zone (Figure 4F) revealed that, on average, 13.5% of targets were labeled #3 or #4, with some extreme instances where the ratio reached 20% or above. Meanwhile, targets labeled #1 with reaction rates of at least 76% (Supplementary Figure S14B) of the ideal ones generally constituted 40−50% of the total targets. This indicates that almost a half of the targets could be filtered out during the energy screening, which may largely reduce the algorithmic complexity of searching for optimal targets.

sec.title: Free energy change outperforms other factors in interpreting trans-cleavage activity
sec.p: Apart from the free energy change of nucleic acids, the efficiency of the CRISPR reaction could be influenced by a variety of other factors, particularly sequence features such as GC content (31,32) and nucleotide preference at each position of the target (31,33,35). However, these findings were based on cis-cleavage studies which were intrinsically affected by sequence composition of the substrate and might therefore be inadequate for explaining the real-time nuclease kinetics reflected by trans-cleavage activity. Using the difference from the highest logarithm of the trans-cleavage rate as the metric, we obtained the distribution of trans-cleavage activity across all levels of GC content. Clearly, for both dsDNA (Figure 5A) and ssDNA targets at all concentrations (Supplementary Figure S18), the variance of trans-cleavage activity was less apparent with GC contents than with divided energy zones, as displayed in Supplementary Figures S12 and S13. However, the trans-cleavage activity generally maintained satisfactory with balanced GC contents, while more targets exhibiting extremely slow trans-cleavage kinetics were observed with extreme GC contents. Due to substantial correlations between the GC content and free energy change of nucleic acids, especially DNA targets and crRNA–DNA hybrids (Supplementary Figure S19), we speculated this obscure relationship between trans-cleavage activity and GC content stemmed from free energy change. Weak trans-cleavage activity for high GC contents could be explained by more energy consumption in spacer or target unwinding, and compromised trans-cleavage activity for low GC contents could potentially be attributed to high leading to a less stable crRNA–DNA duplex, corroborated by previous literature suggesting that targets with insufficient lengths result in Cas12a RNP easily detaching the DNA (54). The effect of target melting temperature can also be understood in this context, as it is deeply associated with GC content and (Supplementary Figure S20). Alternatively, if viewing the R-loop formation as a dynamic and reversible process (55), an interesting explanation for inferior trans-cleavage activity for dsDNA targets with low GC contents was an unfavorable competition for crRNA invasion against dsDNA recovery after PAM-induced separation (26) (Supplementary Figure S21A). Surprisingly, we found a correlation between GC content and the difference between and where smaller compared to mostly occurred when GC content was less than 0.5 (Supplementary Figure S21B), indicating higher stability for targets in duplexed form than the crRNA–DNA hybrid and a stronger inclination for double-strand recovery for low GC content targets. Serendipitously, the variations in trans-cleavage activity with − could be approximated symmetrically in the form of a parabola with an axis of symmetry close to 0, which implied that a balanced point for and was most beneficial to Cas12a activation (Supplementary Figure S21C). Both theories support the finding that high was disadvantageous in trans-cleavage since generally coincided with high and low − (Supplementary Figure S21D, E). Nonetheless, if we considered or − as a third feature in machine learning, the prediction accuracy scores in most situations were not markedly improved for naïve Bayes (Figure 5B) and other models (Supplementary Figure S22), with the division of energy zones generally remaining in the same pattern but occasionally becoming more sketchy and discontinuous (Supplementary Figures S23–S28). These observations suggest a simple two-feature model merely involving and is sufficient for prediction of trans-cleavage activity.

sec.p: We next studied the impact of target sequence composition on Cas12a nuclease activation. To investigate whether there is a preferred pattern of nucleotides at specific positions, we classified target sequences based on their relative trans-cleavage rates to the highest observed with the same target type and concentration, with a logarithm difference of 0.301 (50% of the strongest reactivity) being the threshold. We primarily analyzed the conservation of nucleotides in dsDNA targets due to limited sequence diversity for ssDNA targets studied and an unexpected prevalence of the computationally designed targets ending in ‘G’ and ‘A’. The sequence logo (56) indicated no recognizable nucleotide preference in both high-performance targets (Figure 5C) and low-performance targets (Figure 5D), with an almost even distribution of nucleobases at each position (Supplementary Figure S29), suggesting minimal influence on Cas12a activation by sequence composition. Defining a homopolymer as a segment of the target sequence containing three or more consecutive identical nucleotides, we observed that the difference in the distribution of trans-cleavage activity between the homopolymer and non-homopolymer groups was also unidentifiable regarding the 25th–75th percentile range and median value (Figure 5E). However, more extreme outliers indicating weak trans-cleavage activity were found in the homopolymer group. A detailed analysis of homopolymer types revealed that the extreme outliers were concentrated in targets with ‘C’ and ‘G’ homopolymers (Figure 5F). Defining the seed region as the first six nucleotides immediately adjacent to PAM (36), we were surprised to find that all the extreme outliers corresponded to targets with ‘GGG’s in the seed region and 'CCC’s in the non-seed region (Figure 5G), suggesting the position of such homopolymers may play a role in regulating the kinetics of trans-cleavage activity. We infer that the homopolymer effect may stem from extreme local free energy changes related to only a few nucleotides in the complete sequence, which cannot be captured by the overall free energy changes. To assess this hypothesis, we expanded the concept of homopolymer to include G/C-rich regions with increased local energy barriers for unwinding, and A/T-rich regions which are easier to unwind but may result in local instability of the crRNA/target duplex structure and impact enzyme activity. We defined an 'extreme local energy penalty score’ that increases by 1 for each occurrence of three consecutive ‘A/T’ or ‘G/C’ nucleotides in the 20-nt target sequence. A high penalty score can indicate either the presence of A/T- or G/C-rich regions in many discrete locations, or the existence of long A/T- or G/C-rich regions which may have a greater effect than the short ones. To specifically address the variation in trans-cleavage rates within the optimal overall energy change range, we classified crRNA/target pairs with constrained energy changes ( ≥−2 kcal/mol, −28 kcal/mol ≤ ≤−22 kcal/mol for dsDNA, and ≥−2 kcal/mol for ssDNA), into ‘low penalty score’ and ‘high penalty score’ groups, each containing nearly equal sample sizes. From Figure 5H for the dsDNA dataset, we observed that high penalty scores led to weaker trans-cleavage activity on average, which supports our hypothesis that extreme local free energy changes may negatively affect Cas12a activity. However, the difference between high and low penalty scores becomes less apparent for the ssDNA dataset (Figure 5I), potentially because GC-rich regions not hybridized and a lack of energy favorability for unwound A/T-rich target to recover (Supplementary Figure S21A).

Furthermore, as the repeat domain of crRNAs in this study manifested both the canonical hairpin structures and diverse irregular structures, we were also curious if the conformation of the repeat was a key factor in regulating Cas12a activation. We reviewed the trans-cleavage activity for crRNAs with a high probability (≥75% of suboptimal structures) of retaining a canonical repeat structure or forming an altered repeat structure. Surprisingly, we found that the overall reactivity for crRNAs with noncanonical repeat structures was even slightly higher than those with canonical repeat structures (Figure 5J), suggesting that imperfections in the strictly conserved hairpin structure might not have a presumably negative effect. Analysis of reactivity in each energy zone revealed that Cas12a activation might not have a clear correlation with the repeat structure, as the relative reactivity for these two categories of crRNAs in each cluster seemed arbitrary (Figure 5K). Supported by previous findings demonstrating persistent nuclease activity with modified repeats (57,58) and even with substantial removal of the repeat domain (59), we reasoned that the variations in trans-cleavage activity within and between crRNAs with canonical and noncanonical repeat structures were principally governed by energy consumption for spacer exposure, which peculiarly accounted for the reported reduced activity when spacer-repeat hybridization existed (48). Lastly, we investigated whether the PAM-proximal seed region was crucial in determining the nuclease kinetics of CRISPR-Cas12a system, as suggested by earlier findings (32,35–37). Because it was difficult to recognize a pattern for the prevalence of nucleobases throughout the target sequence (Figure 5C, D), we wondered if the energy consumption during seed region unwinding was a more distinctive feature than the overall energy consumption of target or spacer unwinding. Defining seed region as the first six bases at the PAM-proximal site (36), we computed and , which referred to the free energy change only when the seed in the target or the bases matching the seed in the crRNA became unhybridized. Interestingly, we found that the correlation between free energy change and trans-cleavage activity attenuated when simply considering the seed region, which applied to both the spacer and the target with less satisfactory fitting statistics (Figure 5L−O). Concluding from the above observations, the energy consumption during the unwinding of base pairs in the complete spacer and target sequence outperformed other factors in predicting trans-cleavage activity.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Using computationally designed crRNAs with specified hairpin structures in the spacer domain, we discovered that self-pairing in the spacer was closely related to the weakening of trans-cleavage activity of CRISPR-Cas12a. We deduced that a more fundamental factor controlling the nuclease kinetics was the free energy change, specifically, the energy consumption during the transitioning of crRNA spacer and DNA target from their original states with complex secondary structures to fully unwound states ready for hybridization. We validated this hypothesis using a large quantity of crRNA/DNA pairs with various target types. We concluded that for crRNA targeting ssDNA, less energy consumption for both crRNA and ssDNA generally associates with high trans-cleavage rates but may vary when applying different molar ratios of crRNA and DNA. For crRNA targeting dsDNA, while less energy consumption for crRNA still benefits trans-cleavage kinetics, the ideal energy consumption for dsDNA separation is situated at an intermediate level. Considering the intrinsic correlation between the free energy change of the target and GC content, this finding aligns with the empirical rule that a balanced GC content is the least detrimental to CRISPR nuclease activity. We assume that while the adverse effect with high GC content is related to high energy consumption for target separation, the slightly diminished trans-cleavage activity with low GC content is due to unstable crRNA–DNA binding or an inclination for the separated target to recover and displace the transiently bound crRNA. Moreover, local free energy changes, associated with small segments of the sequence, may refine the energy model and enhance the accuracy of predicting crRNA activity. However, more studies are needed to elucidate this effect through dedicated experimental design.

To accurately generalize the impact of free energy change on trans-cleavage activity, we employed multiple machine learning approaches, which produced clear 2D energy zone divisions regarding the predicted level of reaction rates. The exact values defining the boundaries of each energy zone are computable. Notably, these results may serve as a standard in target selection for the widespread application of Cas12a in nucleic acid detection. With the best prediction model, we classified candidate targets from common viruses, with nearly half of them identified as outliers from the optimal energy zone. We anticipate that eliminating these targets from the pool may significantly reduce the computational complexity for existing and prospective algorithms aimed at identifying the best targets. Moreover, distinct from cis-cleavage, trans-cleavage is less dependent on sequence features such as nucleotide preferences and is not heavily influenced by other latent factors, including repeat domain structure, seed region free energy change, and even the energy release for crRNA–DNA duplex formation. This renders energy consumption of nucleic acid unwinding the major property determining Cas12a nuclease kinetics. We suppose that, unlike numerous studies on cis-cleavage efficiency, the measurement of trans-cleavage rates is more valuable in revealing the real-time activation of CRISPR nucleases. This is because the substrate for trans-cleavage is uniform (5′-TTATT-3′), ensuring that the nuclease activity is not subject to variations at the cleavage site. Nonetheless, analysis of the in vivo cis-cleavage datasets (38,60–64) (Supplementary Table S1), most of which were based on indel frequency measurements, revealed similar correlation between free energy changes and reaction efficiency (Supplementary Figure S30). The analysis showed conformity in energy zones corresponding to optimal CRISPR activity as identified by machine-learning classifications (Supplementary Figure S31), despite a tendency toward low , possibly due to the prolonged reaction period, which favors high gRNA/target stability. Lastly, as indicated by the understanding of CRISPR reactions from an energy perspective demonstrated here, such insights may be extended to all enzymatic reactions involving nucleic acid conformational changes for the analysis and prediction of biochemical reaction efficiency.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: The raw trans-cleavage rate data and the codes used to (1) generate the sequences of crRNAs with certain secondary structures under specific criteria (i.e. constraints on GC content, avoidance of certain patterns that reduce sequence diversity, thresholds of base-pairing probability), as well as generating RPA primers screened for balanced GC content, absence of significant secondary structure, homodimers and heterodimers, and low chance of non-specific amplification on the non-target region of the constructed plasmid; (2) compute the free energy change of crRNA spacers, short DNA targets, long ssDNA targets and dsDNA targets from their MFE states to the unwound states ready for crRNA–DNA hybridization, along with the release of free energy when forming the crRNA–DNA duplexes; (3) implement unsupervised machine learning (K-means clustering) and supervised machine learning (naive Bayes, SVM, LDA, logistic regression and neural network) for the prediction of trans-cleavage activity given the energy data and the creation of energy zones on the 2D map are provided through https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13134656.
